metadata.name: groups
metadata.displayName: groups - Print group names a user belongs to
metadata.description: Print group names a user belongs to

installation.note: groups is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The groups command displays the group memberships for a specified user, or for the current user if no username is provided. It's useful for checking user permissions and understanding which groups a user belongs to, which affects file access and system privileges.
when_to_use: Check which groups the current user belongs to
View group memberships for another user
Verify user permissions and access rights

syntax.description: Without a username, groups displays groups for the current user. With a username, it shows groups for that user.

examples.title: Show current user's groups
examples.description: Display all groups the current user belongs to
examples.output: username : username adm dialout cdrom sudo dip plugdev lpadmin sambashare

elements.meaning: The username (appears twice - once as label, once as primary group)
Administration group - access to system logs

output_explanation.notes: The first group listed is typically the primary group. Other groups are supplementary groups.

examples.use_case: Quick check of your own group memberships

examples.title: Show groups for specific user
examples.description: Display all groups that user 'john' belongs to
examples.use_case: Check another user's group memberships (requires appropriate permissions)

examples.title: Use with environment variable
examples.description: Display groups for the user specified by USER environment variable
examples.use_case: In scripts to check groups for the current user

misconceptions.title: Shows all groups on system
misconceptions.misconception: groups displays all groups on the system
misconceptions.reality: groups only shows groups that the specified user belongs to, not all system groups
misconceptions.tip: Use 'getent group' or 'cat /etc/group' to see all groups on the system

misconceptions.title: Primary vs supplementary groups
misconceptions.misconception: All groups shown have equal importance
misconceptions.reality: The first group is the primary group (GID), others are supplementary groups
misconceptions.tip: Primary group is used for new file creation. Supplementary groups grant additional permissions.

common_pitfalls.description: May not be able to view groups for other users
common_pitfalls.solution: Use 'sudo' if you need to check groups for other users, or use 'id' command which provides similar information

common_pitfalls.description: New group memberships may not appear until user logs out and back in
common_pitfalls.solution: User must log out and log back in, or use 'newgrp' command to activate new groups in current session

related_commands.description: id shows user and group IDs (numeric) in addition to names, and provides more detailed information
whoami shows current username, groups shows that user's groups
getent group shows all groups, getent passwd shows user information
usermod -aG adds users to groups, groups displays the result

best_practices: Use 'groups' without arguments to check your own groups quickly
Combine with 'id' command for more detailed information including numeric IDs
Remember that group changes require re-login to take effect
Use 'newgrp' to temporarily switch primary group in current session
performance_tips: groups is very fast as it only reads /etc/group file
For scripts, 'id -Gn' provides similar output in a more parseable format

additional_notes.primary_group: The first group listed is the primary group (GID), used as default for new files
additional_notes.supplementary_groups: Additional groups grant extra permissions beyond the primary group
additional_notes.group_file: Group information is stored in /etc/group file
